column3: The soul summoned to bless the Lord
column4: Both psalms open with a Davidic designation and the speaker summoning his own soul to bless the Lord. Psalm 102 adds all within him and the holy name; Psalm 103 proceeds to God's greatness and clothing.

column3: Blessing God without forgetting His benefits
column4: The psalm joins blessing the Lord to not forgetting His repayments. Deuteronomy likewise joins blessing God for the good land to warnings against forgetting Him amid received abundance; its material examples remain its own.

column3: Forgiveness and healing brought together
column4: The psalm attributes forgiveness of lawless deeds and healing of diseases to God. Mark brings forgiveness and the paralytic's healing together in Jesus' encounter with him. This compares the paired acts without claiming an explicit quotation or exclusive prediction.

column3: Redemption from corruption and Hades
column4: Psalm 102 blesses the one redeeming life from corruption; Psalm 48 expects God to redeem the speaker's soul from Hades' hand. Both describe divine rescue in relation to death while preserving corruption and Hades as different expressions.

column3: Renewal pictured through an eagle
column4: The psalm describes youth renewed like an eagle. Isaiah describes those enduring for God exchanging strength and growing wings like eagles. The shared renewal and eagle imagery does not make youth and strength identical wording.

column3: God's justice for the wronged
column4: Psalm 102 joins mercy and judgment for all the wronged; Psalm 145 says the Lord does justice for those wronged. The common recipients and judicial action provide the particular correspondence.

column3: Divine instruction through Moses to Israel
column4: The psalm says God made His ways known to Moses and His wishes to Israel's sons. Moses in Deuteronomy says he showed Israel ordinances and judgments as the Lord commanded him. The comparison concerns that named channel of instruction, with the different terms preserved.

column3: The compassionate and merciful Lord
column4: The psalm repeats the cluster compassionate, merciful, slow to anger and abundant in mercy found in the Lord's proclamation before Moses. Exodus additionally calls Him true; that addition is not imported into this source unit.

column3: Anger that does not last forever
column4: The psalm denies enduring anger and perpetual wrath; Isaiah's divine speech denies taking vengeance forever or always being angry. The parallel concerns the stated temporal limit, without equating every recipient or surrounding circumstance.

column3: Heavenly height and the greatness of mercy
column4: Psalm 102 uses heaven's height above earth to describe mercy strengthened toward those fearing God. Psalm 56 says mercy was magnified to the heavens. The height imagery corresponds while their prepositions and statements about recipients remain distinct.

column3: Sins removed through a spatial image
column4: The psalm measures removal of lawless deeds by the distance of east from west. Micah depicts sins thrown into the sea's depths. Both use great spatial separation to portray removal of sins, with horizontal distance and depth kept distinct.

column3: Fatherhood and divine compassion
column4: The psalm compares the Lord's compassion with a father's compassion for children. Isaiah's prayer asks about withheld compassion and confesses God as Father. The psalm states compassion; the prayer seeks it amid felt deprivation.

column3: Human formation and dust
column4: The psalm connects knowledge of human formation with the imperative to remember that we are dust. Genesis narrates God forming the human from earth's dust. The source's imperative is preserved rather than changed into a statement that God remembers dust.

column3: Human life as grass and a field flower
column4: Both passages compare human life or glory with grass and a flower. Isaiah explicitly describes their withering and contrasts God's enduring word; Psalm 102 places the flower image within its account of short human life.

column3: Vanishing life and the unrecognized place
column4: The psalm's mortal no longer recognizes his place after passing away; Job says the dead person's place will no longer recognize him. The unusual place-recognition image corresponds, but its subject and object are reversed and remain distinct.

column3: Mercy for those fearing God across generations
column4: Both associate God's mercy with those fearing Him and extend the description across generations. The psalm also mentions righteousness for children's children; Luke places its declaration in Mary's song.

column3: Mercy and commandment keeping within covenant
column4: The psalm describes covenant keepers who remember commands to do them. Deuteronomy describes God keeping covenant and mercy with those loving Him and keeping His commands. The actors of covenant keeping differ, while the recipients' obedience corresponds.

column3: The Lord's heavenly throne
column4: Both locate the Lord's throne in heaven. Psalm 102 connects it with universal kingship; Psalm 10 proceeds to His examination of human beings. The shared throne location supports the comparison without merging the following claims.

column3: Angels summoned to praise God
column4: Psalm 102 commands the Lord's angels to bless Him and describes their obedience. Psalm 148 commands all His angels to praise Him. The common summons and named recipients correspond; the obedience description belongs to Psalm 102.

column3: All God's powers summoned to praise
column4: Psalm 102 summons all the Lord's powers to bless Him, describing ministers doing His will. Psalm 148 likewise summons all His powers to praise Him. The shared group and act support the link without interpreting powers beyond the wording.

column3: Same-chapter closing return to the soul's blessing
column4: After summoning angels, powers and all works, the final unit returns to the opening summons for the speaker's soul to bless the Lord. This same-chapter comparison identifies the psalm's closing return to its opening address.

column3: The soul summoned to bless the Lord
column4: The two openings share a Davidic designation and the summons for the speaker's soul to bless the Lord. Their following praise differs: God's greatness and clothing here, the holy name and all within the speaker in Psalm 102.

column3: Heaven stretched like a covering
column4: The psalm describes heaven stretched like a hide curtain; Isaiah says God stretched it like a tent for dwelling. The fabric-covering comparison and divine action correspond, with Isaiah's vault and the psalm's light garment retained as separate details.

column3: Divine movement on the wings of winds
column4: Both describe God moving on the wings of winds. Psalm 17 also names cherubim and flight; Psalm 103 speaks of upper chambers and clouds as a means of ascent. These additional images are not collapsed into one description.

column3: Angels and fiery ministers in a cited saying
column4: Hebrews introduces a saying concerning angels that closely follows this psalm's angels and fiery ministers. The psalm says winds and burning fire, while Hebrews says spirits and a flame of fire; the textual differences are preserved within the quotation relationship.

column3: The established earth that will not be shaken
column4: Psalm 103 describes the earth founded in stability and not tilted for ages. Psalm 92 describes the inhabited world established so it will not be shaken. Both connect divine establishment with lasting stability, preserving their different nouns and verbs.

column3: Waters above the mountains
column4: The psalm pictures the deep as a covering and says waters will stand upon mountains; Genesis narrates floodwaters covering high mountains. The particular water-over-mountains image corresponds without establishing that the psalm identifies the same historical event or tense.

column3: Thunder and divine rebuke before the waters
column4: Psalm 103 depicts waters fleeing at God's rebuke and fearing His thunderous voice. Psalm 17 joins heavenly thunder with waters' springs appearing at His rebuke. The shared rebuke, thunder and water imagery is retained without equating fleeing with appearing.

column3: The boundary waters cannot cross
column4: The psalm says God set a boundary the waters will not pass. Job's divine speech describes setting sea boundaries and declaring that it will not pass beyond them. The imposed limit is particular; the psalm's further prevention of earth-covering remains its own.

column3: Springs flowing through varied terrain
column4: The psalm describes springs sent into ravines and water passing between mountains. Deuteronomy describes the good land's torrents and deep springs flowing through plains and hills. The shared springs and terrain pattern is compared without identifying the psalm's entire scene with that land.

column3: Hills watered from above
column4: The psalm describes God watering mountains from His upper chambers. Deuteronomy describes a land of hills and plains drinking heaven's rain and receiving God's care. Both connect elevated terrain with water from above, while the upper-chamber image remains the psalm's.

column3: Grass for cattle and food for people
column4: Both passages connect God's provision of grass for cattle with human food. Deuteronomy names grain, wine and oil and then grass and human eating; the psalm names green plants for human service and bread from earth.

column3: Wine as human gladness
column4: The psalm says wine gladdens the human heart. In Jotham's tree parable the vine calls its wine human beings' gladness from God. The shared function of wine is particular; the parable does not supply the psalm's separate oil and bread statements.

column3: God planting a cedar
column4: The psalm names Lebanon's cedars as trees God planted. Ezekiel's divine speech describes taking and planting a cedar shoot on Israel's mountain. The same tree and divine planting provide the comparison, without equating the natural description with the prophetic planting scene.

column3: A sparrow and the provision of a home
column4: Psalm 103 describes sparrows nesting; Psalm 83 describes a sparrow finding a house alongside a turtledove's nest at God's altars. The nesting and housing comparison preserves the different settings and birds and does not interpret the separate heron's-house clause.

column3: Rock as an animal refuge and dwelling
column4: The psalm calls rock a refuge for rock rabbits; Proverbs describes rock badgers making houses in rocks. The particular rocky dwelling imagery corresponds. The different animal names are preserved, and their zoological identity is not established by this retained comparison.

column3: Heavenly lights marking time
column4: The psalm names the moon's seasons and the sun's setting. Genesis describes heavenly lights for seasons, days and years, with greater and lesser lights ruling day and night. The shared ordering of time is retained with their different naming and functions explicit.

column3: Darkness and the ordering of night
column4: The psalm addresses God as setting darkness so that night comes; Genesis describes God dividing light from darkness and naming darkness Night. The relation concerns the divine ordering of darkness and night; the forest beasts occur only in the psalm.

column3: Lions and provision of their food
column4: The psalm says young lions seek their food from God. The Lord asks Job whether he will hunt food for lions, also mentioning dragons. The particular feeding question is compared with the psalm's statement, without turning Job's question into an identical assertion.

column3: The earth's making through wisdom
column4: Psalm 103 says God made all His works in wisdom and the earth is filled with His possession. Proverbs says God founded the earth by wisdom. The shared wisdom-and-earth creation claim supports the link while retaining the psalm's wider scope.

column3: The sea's multitude of living creatures
column4: The psalm portrays a spacious sea containing innumerable moving creatures, small and great. Genesis narrates the waters bringing forth moving life and God making great sea creatures. The marine-life description corresponds without identifying every creature or equating the inventories.

column3: A remarkable creature formed for play
column4: The psalm's sea dragon is formed to play with it; Job's creature, identified as a dragon in the preceding discourse, is made to be played with by God's angels. The unusual formation-and-play relation is retained without importing the angels into the psalm or settling zoological identity.

column3: All creatures awaiting food at the right time
column4: Both describe all looking or waiting toward God and receiving food at the right time. Psalm 144 specifies their eyes hoping; Psalm 103 follows its account of the sea's creatures. The shared dependence and timing form the close comparison.

column3: God's opened hand filling living creatures
column4: Both associate God's opened hand with creatures being filled. Psalm 103 says all are filled with goodness and also gather what He gives; Psalm 144 names every living creature and good pleasure. The distinctions remain within the close shared image.

column3: Death and return to dust
column4: The psalm describes withdrawal of breath, failure and return to dust. Ecclesiastes describes dust returning to earth and spirit returning to God who gave it. The bodily return corresponds, while breath and spirit and the direction of their movement are not made identical.

column3: Divine spirit and the making of life
column4: The psalm says creatures are created when God sends His spirit. Elihu says divine spirit made him. The common creative role of spirit supports the comparison; his additional statement that the Almighty's breath teaches him is not rewritten as giving life.

column3: God rejoicing in what He makes
column4: The psalm asks that the Lord rejoice in His works. Isaiah joins God's making Jerusalem an exultation and His people joy with His rejoicing over them. The creative delight corresponds, with the psalm's broad works and Isaiah's specific people and city kept distinct.

column3: Mountains smoking at God's touch
column4: Both connect God's touching mountains with their smoking. Psalm 103 describes this within praise of His power; Psalm 143 asks Him to descend and touch them. The uncommon action and effect correspond despite statement and petition differing.

column3: Lifelong praise and music to God
column4: Both promise praise to the Lord throughout life and music to God while the speaker exists. The paired lifelong commitments provide a close verbal and structural correspondence.

column3: Pleasing expression and meditation before God
column4: Psalm 103 desires meditation sweet to God. Psalm 18 describes pleasing sayings of the mouth and heart-meditation continually before Him. The paired inward reflection and pleasing expression correspond, while the grammatical objects of sweetness and pleasure remain different.

column3: Removal of the lawless from the earth
column4: Psalm 103 desires sinners to vanish from earth and the lawless no longer to exist. Proverbs says ungodly ways perish from the land and the lawless are driven out. The lawless and their removal correspond; ways, people, extinction and expulsion are not conflated.

column3: Same-chapter return to the opening blessing
column4: The last unit returns to the opening summons for the speaker's soul to bless the Lord after the creation praise and wish concerning sinners. This same-chapter comparison marks the deliberate framing summons.

column3: Thanksgiving and making God's works known
column4: Both summon thanksgiving, calling on God's name and making His works known among peoples or nations. Chronicles places the closely corresponding summons in the praise David appointed through Asaph and his brethren.

column3: Singing and recounting divine wonders
column4: Both command song or music to God and recounting His wonders. Chronicles additionally says to recount them to everyone and identifies them as what the Lord has done.

column3: The holy name and a rejoicing seeker
column4: Both join the holy name with a seeking heart's rejoicing. The psalm says be praised and speaks of seeking the Lord; Chronicles says praise and speaks of seeking His good pleasure. Those differences remain explicit.

column3: Seeking the Lord and His face continually
column4: Both join seeking the Lord, being strengthened and seeking His face continually. This shared sequence is the particular correspondence.

column3: Remembering wonders, portents and judgments
column4: Both command remembrance of God's wonders, portents and the judgments of His mouth. The three-part sequence supports a close parallel within the two praise passages.

column3: The addressed offspring and chosen sons of Jacob
column4: Both address servants and Jacob's chosen sons. The psalm calls the offspring Abraham's, whereas Chronicles calls them Israel's. The corresponding address is retained without silently replacing either ancestral name.

column3: Our God and His judgments throughout earth
column4: Both confess Him as the Lord our God and locate His judgments throughout the earth. The corresponding confession follows the addressed ancestral offspring in each passage.

column3: The remembered covenant and a thousand generations
column4: Both connect God's remembrance of His covenant with the word commanded for a thousand generations. The psalm says He remembered; Chronicles says He remembers. Their closely shared content is retained with tense distinguished.

column3: Covenant with Abraham and oath to Isaac
column4: Both name Abraham in the covenant statement and Isaac in the oath statement. The matching named recipients and parallel arrangement provide the direct correspondence.

column3: The ordinance for Jacob and everlasting covenant for Israel
column4: Both describe establishment for Jacob as an ordinance and for Israel as an everlasting covenant. This closely matching two-part formulation is retained without adding a different covenant episode.

column3: Canaan as the measured inheritance
column4: Both quote the promise of Canaan as the measured allotment of inheritance. The named land and measured-inheritance language make the connection particular.

column3: Few and small strangers in the land
column4: Both describe the ancestral group as few, small and dwelling as strangers. The corresponding combination occurs at the same point after the promise of the land.

column3: Travel from nation to nation
column4: Both describe movement from nation to nation and from a kingdom to another people. The paired travel formula connects the accounts of ancestral wandering.

column3: Protection from wrong and rebuke of kings
column4: Both describe divine protection of the wandering group and rebuke or reproof of kings on their account. The psalm's wronging and Chronicles' overpowering are preserved as different descriptions of the prevented harm.

column3: A king warned in protection of Abraham's household
column4: The psalm recalls kings rebuked on the ancestors' behalf. Genesis narrates God's warning to Abimelech concerning Sarah and identifies Abraham as a prophet. This is a concrete instance within that ancestral history, not a claim that every rebuke refers only to this event.

column3: The prohibition on touching anointed ones and harming prophets
column4: Both give the prohibition on touching God's anointed ones and acting wickedly against His prophets. The matching two-part command is retained without identifying additional named individuals beyond their contexts.

column3: The famine of Joseph's history under God's determination
column4: The psalm says God called famine upon the land before recounting Joseph. Genesis presents Joseph's announcement of the coming severe famine as what God will make true and hasten. The psalm's shattered support of bread remains its own image.

column3: Joseph sold yet sent ahead by God
column4: The psalm joins Joseph's sale into slavery with God's sending a man ahead. Joseph tells his brothers that they sold him but God sent him before them to preserve life. The named person and both actions provide the close narrative correspondence.

column3: Joseph's confinement
column4: The psalm describes Joseph's fettered feet and soul passing through iron. Genesis names Joseph's placement among the king's prisoners. The connection is the same named prisoner's confinement; Genesis does not supply the fetter or iron descriptions.

column3: The ruler sending for Joseph from confinement
column4: The psalm describes the king sending and releasing Joseph. Genesis records Pharaoh sending for him and Joseph being brought out of the fortress. The royal summons and departure from confinement correspond without importing the psalm's wording into Genesis.

column3: Joseph appointed over the ruler's house
column4: The psalm describes Joseph's appointment over the house and possessions. Pharaoh places him over his house and all Egypt. The house appointment and extended authority correspond, with possessions and territory retained as different formulations.

column3: Jacob and Israel entering Egypt
column4: The psalm names Israel's entrance into Egypt and Jacob's sojourn in Ham's land. Genesis narrates Jacob and his descendants entering Egypt. The named migration supplies the link; Ham's designation belongs to the psalm.

column3: Israel's multiplication and strength in Egypt
column4: The psalm says God increased His people and made them stronger than their enemies. Exodus describes Israel multiplying and growing strong, followed by the Egyptian king calling them stronger than his nation. The growth and relative strength correspond.

column3: Crafty hostility toward the multiplying people
column4: The psalm attributes the turn of hearts toward hatred and deceit to God. Exodus records the king proposing crafty treatment and the Egyptians loathing Israel. The hostility and deceit correspond; Exodus does not explicitly attribute that heart-turning to God in these units.

column3: Moses and Aaron commissioned for Israel's departure
column4: The psalm names the sending of Moses and chosen Aaron. Exodus identifies Aaron and Moses as those God commanded to bring Israel out and who spoke to Pharaoh. The named commission supports the connection without transferring every title between accounts.

column3: Signs and wonders in Egypt
column4: The psalm attributes words of signs and portents in Ham's land to the commissioned pair. Exodus's divine speech promises multiplied signs and wonders in Egypt through the confrontation with Pharaoh. The setting and signs correspond, preserving the psalm's words formulation.

column3: The Egyptian darkness
column4: Both describe the divinely sent darkness in Egypt. Exodus specifies its duration and the Israelites' light. The psalm's positive clause that they provoked His words is preserved and is not rewritten as an assertion that they did not rebel.

column3: Water turned to blood and fish killed
column4: Both join waters turning to blood with the death of fish in Egypt. Exodus narrates the striking of the river; the psalm condenses the two linked effects.

column3: Frogs reaching the ruler's chambers
column4: The psalm describes frogs in the land and kings' chambers. The warning to Pharaoh describes frogs entering houses, bedchambers and beds. The unusual invasion of sleeping chambers connects the plague descriptions, with plural kings and Pharaoh's address distinguished.

column3: Gnats across Egypt
column4: The psalm's command brings gnats within their borders alongside dog-flies. Exodus narrates gnats arising throughout Egypt after Aaron strikes the dust. This comparison concerns the gnat component, not a claim that both plagues occurred simultaneously in Exodus.

column3: Dog-flies across Egypt
column4: The psalm names dog-flies alongside gnats. Exodus narrates a multitude of dog-flies entering Pharaoh's and his attendants' houses and ruining the land. This comparison concerns the distinct dog-fly component of the psalm's compressed account.

column3: Hail accompanied by fire
column4: Both join hail in Egypt with fire. Exodus explicitly describes fire flaming amid hail, while the psalm describes rain made hail and consuming fire. The combined phenomena provide the particular correspondence.

column3: The hail's destruction of trees
column4: The psalm names struck vines and fig trees and shattered trees. Exodus describes hail shattering trees and striking plants in the plains. The destructive effect on trees corresponds; the specific vines and figs are not supplied by the target unit.

column3: The arrival of innumerable locusts
column4: The psalm describes locusts and larvae coming at God's word without number. Exodus narrates the Lord's wind bringing locusts in unprecedented numbers over Egypt. The locust arrival and multitude correspond, with larvae remaining an additional psalm term.

column3: Locusts consuming vegetation and fruit
column4: Both describe locust devastation of the land's vegetation and fruit. Exodus specifies what the hail had left and the absence of remaining greenery; the psalm compresses the consumption into its account of the plague.

column3: The striking of Egypt's firstborn
column4: Both describe the striking of every firstborn in Egypt. Exodus names the range from Pharaoh's firstborn to a captive woman's and livestock; the psalm uses the additional expression firstfruits of their toil.

column3: Silver and gold in Israel's departure
column4: The psalm describes bringing Israel out with silver and gold. Exodus narrates Israel asking for these articles and receiving Egyptian favor. The valuables connect the departure accounts; the psalm's absence of weakness among the tribes is not asserted by the target.

column3: Egypt's fear and eagerness for Israel's departure
column4: The psalm says Egypt rejoiced at Israel's going because fear had fallen upon them. Exodus says Egyptians pressed for rapid departure, fearing that all were dying. Their desire for departure and fear correspond, while joy and the quoted fear of death remain distinct.

column3: Cloud and night fire during the departure
column4: Both recall cloud and night fire accompanying Israel. The psalm calls the cloud a shelter and the fire illumination; Exodus describes guiding pillars of cloud and fire. Their respective functions and forms are preserved.

column3: Quail and bread in the wilderness
column4: The psalm pairs quail with bread from heaven. Exodus narrates quail in the evening and the next morning's fine substance identified as bread given by the Lord. The paired foods connect these wilderness-provision accounts.

column3: Water coming from the rock
column4: The psalm describes a split rock and waters flowing in a waterless place. Exodus commands the striking of the rock at Horeb so water will come out for the people, and records Moses doing so. The rock-water provision corresponds without equating every descriptive detail.

column3: Divine remembrance involving Abraham
column4: The psalm says God remembered His holy word to Abraham. Exodus says God remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob upon hearing Israel's groaning. The named ancestor and remembrance within the deliverance history provide the connection, with word and covenant distinguished.

column3: Celebration within Israel's deliverance from Egypt
column4: The psalm recalls bringing the people out in exultation and gladness. Exodus depicts Miriam leading the women with timbrels, dances and song after the sea rescue. That particular celebration illustrates joy within the deliverance history without making all participants or timing identical.

column3: Receiving what others had built and cultivated
column4: The psalm says Israel inherited the nations' toils. Deuteronomy describes receiving cities, houses, cisterns, vineyards and olive groves Israel did not build, fill, hew or plant. Those concrete unearned works illuminate the psalm's inheritance description.

column3: Keeping ordinances in the inherited land
column4: The psalm gives keeping ordinances and seeking God's law as the purpose following the land gift. Moses describes ordinances and judgments to be carried out in the land Israel will inherit. The shared land-and-obedience connection is retained with their different temporal perspectives.

column3: Thanksgiving and enduring mercy
column4: Both summon thanksgiving to the Lord and affirm His mercy forever. The psalm says He is good; Chronicles says it is good. The closely matching refrain is preserved without silently replacing the different pronoun.

column3: Recounting God's immeasurable deeds
column4: Psalm 105 asks who will speak the Lord's mighty deeds and make all His praises heard. Psalm 39 describes announcing God's wonders, which multiplied beyond number. The comparison concerns the extent of recounting, preserving question and declaration as different forms.

column3: Blessedness joined to justice and righteousness
column4: The psalm blesses those keeping judgment and doing righteousness at all times. Isaiah commands keeping justice and doing righteousness, then pronounces happiness on the person doing these things. The paired actions and blessing closely correspond.

column3: God visiting His people in salvation
column4: The psalm petitions God to remember the people and visit them in His salvation. Zechariah blesses God for having visited and accomplished redemption for His people. The visitation and people correspond, while petition and reported accomplishment differ.

column3: God's chosen nation as His inheritance
column4: Psalm 105 seeks the good and joy of God's chosen ones, nation and inheritance. Psalm 32 blesses the nation whose God is the Lord and the people He chose as His inheritance. The distinctive chosen-people and inheritance cluster supports the comparison.

column3: The communal confession of sin and wrongdoing
column4: The psalm confesses sin, lawlessness and injustice, associating the speakers with their fathers. Solomon's prayer gives a closely corresponding threefold confession for captives returning to God. The shared confession is retained without adding the fathers clause to the target.

column3: Israel's complaint in the Red Sea deliverance
column4: The psalm recalls ancestral provocation while going up in the Red Sea. Exodus records the people's complaint about leaving Egypt before the crossing. The comparison locates complaint within that deliverance history while preserving the different placement in the accounts.

column3: Deliverance from Egypt for God's name
column4: The psalm says God saved for His name's sake to make His power known. Ezekiel says He brought Israel out of Egypt so His name would not be profaned before the nations. The divine-name rationale corresponds, with manifestation of power and avoidance of profanation distinguished.

column3: A dry passage through the sea
column4: Both describe the sea made dry and Israel led through it. The psalm describes God's rebuke and passage as through wilderness; Exodus describes Moses' outstretched hand and a violent south wind. The means are not replaced with each other's wording.

column3: Passage through the deep pictured as wilderness travel
column4: The psalm describes guidance through the depths as through wilderness. Isaiah describes overpowering water before Moses and leading through the abyss like a horse through wilderness. The unusual deep-and-wilderness travel comparison is retained without importing the horse into the psalm.

column3: Israel rescued from the enemy's hand
column4: The psalm describes rescue and redemption from the hands of haters and an enemy. Exodus states that the Lord rescued Israel from the Egyptians' hand on the sea-deliverance day. The shared hand-rescue statement is anchored in the same narrated setting.

column3: The pursuers covered with none remaining
column4: Both state that returning waters covered the pursuing force and not one remained. Exodus specifies chariots, riders and Pharaoh's force; the psalm calls them those afflicting Israel.

column3: Trust following the sea deliverance
column4: The psalm says the people believed His words after the waters covered their enemies. Exodus says they trusted God and Moses after seeing what the Lord had done. The response at the same point in the narrative corresponds, with the stated objects of trust distinguished.

column3: Israel's song after the sea rescue
column4: The psalm pairs belief with singing God's praise. Exodus narrates Moses and Israel singing to God after the sea deliverance. This link concerns the song component of the psalm's paired response.

column3: Forgetting divine works within Israel's history
column4: Psalm 105 says the people quickly forgot God's works and did not await His counsel. Psalm 77 recounts forgetting His benefits and the wonders He showed them. Both historical recitals identify forgetting divine acts, without importing the timing or counsel clause into the target.

column3: The wilderness craving for food
column4: The psalm describes an intense desire in the wilderness and testing God. Numbers narrates intense craving and Israel's weeping for meat while remembering Egyptian foods. The distinctive craving within the wilderness provision history connects the accounts.

column3: The desired food supplied in abundance
column4: The psalm says God gave their request and sent fullness to their souls. Numbers describes quail supplied by the Lord's wind and gathered in great quantities after the request for meat. Fullness is preserved; the following plague is not substituted for the psalm's actual wording.

column3: Opposition to Moses and Aaron
column4: Both name Moses and Aaron as the targets of the congregation's antagonism. The psalm calls Aaron the Lord's holy one; Numbers quotes the challengers calling the whole congregation holy. These different attributions of holiness are preserved.

column3: The earth swallowing the rebel households
column4: The psalm names Dathan and Abiram's assembly as swallowed or covered by earth. Numbers narrates the ground splitting and swallowing those just identified with Dathan and Abiram in the surrounding account. The shared event is retained without replacing Numbers' additional Korah designation.

column3: Fire consuming the rebellious assembly
column4: The psalm describes fire in the assembly and a flame burning sinners. Numbers narrates fire from the Lord consuming the two hundred fifty incense presenters in that rebellion. The particular fiery judgment corresponds, while the number and incense belong to Numbers.

column3: The calf and worship of the made image
column4: The psalm describes the calf at Horeb and bowing to a carved image. Exodus narrates making a cast calf and later explicitly recounts bowing and sacrificing to it. The calf worship corresponds, while carved and cast and the source's Horeb name are preserved.

column3: Glory exchanged for a creature's likeness
column4: The psalm describes exchanging glory for the likeness of a grass-eating calf. Romans describes exchanging God's incorruptible glory for an image's likeness involving humans and animals. The exchange and likeness formula is particular, with its objects and scope distinguished.

column3: Forgetting the God who brought Israel from Egypt
column4: The psalm accuses the people of forgetting the God who saved them and did great things in Egypt. Deuteronomy warns against forgetting the Lord who brought them from Egypt's bondage. The named deliverance and forgetting connect accusation with warning.

column3: Wonders in Egypt and passage through the sea
column4: Psalm 105 recalls wonders in Ham's land and fearful acts at the Red Sea. Psalm 77 joins Egyptian wonders with the sea torn apart for passage. The two-part historical sequence corresponds, while Tanis and the skin-bag image remain the target's details.

column3: Moses interceding against threatened destruction
column4: The psalm says Moses stood in the breach to turn away anger when destruction was threatened. Exodus narrates that threat, Moses' plea to cease fierce anger and the Lord's being appeased. The intercession corresponds; the breach is the psalm's image.

column3: The good land refused in unbelief
column4: The psalm says the desirable land was treated as nothing and God's word not believed. Numbers pairs the explorers' declaration of the land's goodness with the congregation's rejection and God's accusation of unbelief. The land and unbelief together identify the particular episode.

column3: The congregation's wilderness grumbling
column4: The psalm describes grumbling in dwellings and not hearing God's voice. Numbers narrates the congregation grumbling against Moses and Aaron and proposing return to Egypt in the land-refusal episode. The complaint is connected without adding the dwelling location to Numbers.

column3: The judgment of falling in the wilderness
column4: The psalm describes a raised hand against the people to cast them down in the wilderness. Numbers announces that their bodies will fall there and that they will not enter the land. Its hand stretched toward settlement is not confused with the psalm's hand against them.

column3: Dispersion among nations and countries
column4: The psalm speaks of casting offspring among nations and scattering them through countries. Ezekiel's wilderness address to the children records the raised hand to scatter and disperse among nations and countries. The paired dispersion language and wilderness context are particular.

column3: Baal-Peor and eating idol sacrifices
column4: Both connect participation in Baal-Peor's worship with eating sacrifices. Numbers calls them sacrifices of idols; the psalm calls them sacrifices of the dead. The shared named cult and meal correspond without resolving that difference by substitution.

column3: The punitive aftermath of Baal-Peor
column4: The psalm says provocation through their practices was followed by multiplied falling. Numbers counts twenty-four thousand deaths in the plague after Baal-Peor. The named episode's harmful aftermath connects the accounts, with the psalm's falling and Numbers' deaths stated distinctly.

column3: Phinehas rising and the harm ceasing
column4: The psalm describes Phinehas standing, making atonement and the breaking ceasing. Numbers names Phinehas rising, narrates his violent intervention and says the plague stopped. The person, intervention and cessation correspond without replacing the psalm's terms with the target's details.

column3: An act reckoned as righteousness
column4: The psalm says Phinehas' intervention was reckoned to him as righteousness; Genesis says Abram believed God and it was reckoned to him as righteousness. The distinctive reckoning formula is shared, while the persons and preceding acts remain different.

column3: Enduring recognition concerning Phinehas
column4: The psalm extends the reckoning of righteousness through generations forever. Numbers promises Phinehas and his seed an everlasting priestly covenant following his atonement. The lasting recognition of the named person's act corresponds without equating righteousness with priesthood.

column3: The disputed waters and harm to Moses
column4: The psalm connects provocation at the water of contradiction with harm to Moses. Numbers names the Water of Dispute and announces that Moses and Aaron will not lead the congregation into the land. The site and consequence correspond while Numbers' accusation of unbelief remains explicit.

column3: Speech at the disputed waters
column4: The psalm says his spirit was embittered and he issued a command with his lips after naming Moses. Numbers records the address Listen to me to the disobedient people at the rock. This connects speech within the episode without rewriting the psalm as an explicit statement about rash words.

column3: The nations remaining in Israel's land
column4: The psalm says Israel did not destroy the nations as commanded. Judges records Canaanites subjected to tribute but not completely removed and remaining among Israel. The unremoved population connects the historical descriptions, while destroy and remove are kept distinct.

column3: Living among nations and adopting their worship
column4: The psalm joins mixing with the nations to learning their works. Judges describes Israel dwelling among named nations, intermarrying and serving their gods. The coexistence and adopted practice provide the connection without reducing every learned work to intermarriage.

column3: Serving other gods as a stumbling block
column4: The psalm says serving carved images became a stumbling block. Exodus warns that serving the resident peoples' gods will be a stumbling block. The unusual service-and-stumbling formulation connects the accusation with the warning.

column3: Sacrificing to demons
column4: Both describe sacrifices offered to demons. The psalm explicitly names sons and daughters as the victims; Deuteronomy contrasts demons with God and discusses unfamiliar gods. The common recipients of sacrifice support the link without adding child victims to Deuteronomy.

column3: Sons and daughters in destructive cult practice
column4: The psalm condemns sacrificing sons and daughters to demons. Jeremiah condemns an altar at Topheth for burning sons and daughters. The shared child-directed cult practice is compared without equating all occasions or importing Topheth, fire and the explicit prohibition into the psalm.

column3: Shed blood staining the land with murder
column4: The psalm says the land was murdered with innocent blood from child sacrifice. Numbers says shed blood stains the land with murder and gives a legal remedy. The unusual land, blood and murder formulation corresponds; the psalm does not state that remedy here.

column3: Prostitution and defilement in Israel's conduct
column4: The psalm joins defilement through works with prostitution through practices. Hosea attributes prostitution to Ephraim and defilement to Israel. The paired indictments correspond without making their historical occasions or named groups identical.

column3: Wrath following Israel's idolatry
column4: The psalm reports the Lord's anger against His people after their idolatry. Judges' overview likewise reports His anger against Israel after their service of other gods. The corresponding stage in that historical cycle is the link; abhorring the inheritance is the psalm's additional description.

column3: Israel handed into enemy power
column4: Both describe God handing Israel over into hostile power. The psalm speaks of nations and hateful masters; Judges names plunderers and surrounding enemies. The divine handover and enemy domination correspond with the descriptions distinguished.

column3: Hostile hands and Israel's affliction
column4: The psalm describes enemies afflicting Israel and humbling them under their hands. Judges joins sale into enemies' hands with the Lord's hand bringing harm and great affliction. The subjection and affliction correspond, while the different immediate agents are preserved.

column3: Repeated rescue followed by renewed disobedience
column4: The psalm summarizes many rescues followed by provocation and humiliation in sins. Judges describes rescue through judges and renewed corruption when a judge died. The recurring rescue-and-relapse pattern is particular; the psalm does not name each judge or episode.

column3: Affliction heard and relief granted
column4: The psalm says God saw the people's affliction when He heard their petition. Judges says He was moved by groaning before those besieging and harming them and saved through the judge. The response to oppressed people's cry corresponds, with petition and groaning distinguished.

column3: Covenant remembrance amid enemy captivity
column4: The psalm connects covenant remembrance and changed purpose with abundant mercy. Leviticus promises not to consume the people or dissolve the covenant in enemies' land and to remember the former covenant. The remembrance and mercy correspond without inserting changed-purpose wording into Leviticus.

column3: Compassion before the captors
column4: The psalm says God granted the people compassion before those taking them captive. Solomon's prayer asks God to grant compassion before captors so they will show compassion. The specific captor-directed mercy corresponds as report and petition.

column3: Rescue from nations and praise of the holy name
column4: Both ask God's saving rescue in relation to the nations so the people may praise His holy name and glory in His praise. The psalm explicitly asks gathering; Chronicles says rescue. Their closely corresponding petitions retain that distinction.

column3: The closing blessing and the people's response
column4: Both bless the Lord, Israel's God, through the ages and call for the people's response. The psalm has May it be twice, while Chronicles has Amen once and then reports praise. The shared closing form is retained with those differences explicit.
